name: Morocco Red
lede: Morocco Red is a dark reddish brown named for Morocco, the North African country whose goatskin leather, tanned and dyed this color, gave English the word morocco for fine bookbinding leather.

sections.title: Leather and a plate
sections.body:
Morocco leather is a sumac-tanned goatskin long associated with Morocco and prized since at least the seventeenth century for bookbindings, often dyed a dark brownish red close to this swatch [3]. Ridgway's 1912 color standards plate this exact red on plate I, hue 5, with the Munsell notation 9.9R 3.4/6.4 [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary files it as a moderate reddish brown, only 2.5 units from that block's center[1].

Its nearest named neighbors are Garnet Brown, 2.8 units away, and Deep Orange-Coloured Brown, 3.0 units away [1]. The plain name [[morocco]] in our library names a lighter, more orange leather tone than this darker red [1]. It sits close in hue to [[burnt-umber]] and [[bole]], two other brown-reds tied to dye and pigment history [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Morocco Red covers at least five percent of the canvas in 1,241 works, over five percent of the whole archive[2]. The earliest dated example is a mural fragment of a Maguey bloodletting ritual from around the year 500, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1450s, in 22 of 109 paintings, almost six times the archive's overall rate for that decade, and paintings from Tibet carry it four and a half times the baseline rate [2]. Filippino Lippi carries it in four of his fourteen paintings here and Albrecht Dürer in twelve of forty-seven, both well above the baseline [2]. It shares a canvas with [[brick]] more than any other color word, six and a half times the baseline [2]. These are computed color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not an identification of any specific pigment [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
